_method.rule: An option is eliminated when a bound follows from the stem using knowledge the item does NOT test: physical plausibility / order of magnitude, positivity, monotonicity, the range of a named function, parity or divisibility, or a trivially forced total. A bound that requires the item's own target insight is NOT free and does not reduce the survivor count; where it would, it is recorded in issues instead.
_method.keys: All 24 keys were re-derived by hand from the stem before running any script. The batch's own solve/distractor_solve fields were executed afterward as a cross-check only; the checker was mutation-tested (a flipped key and a perturbed distractor_solve both fire).

AM15F-01.bounds: f(x)=|2x+5|-3 >= -3 for every x, so any option below -3 is impossible. -10 is out. 4, 10, 14 all survive; parity does not discriminate (all four are even).

AM15F-02.bounds: No free bound. The vertex x-coordinate forces b=-6 in one step, but recovering c needs the vertex y-coordinate, which is the item. c-b is unconstrained without that work; all of -1, 3, 11, 15 are reachable values of c-b for some parabola.

AM15F-03.bounds: None. f is linear (f(u)=3u+2) but nothing in the stem bounds f(7) without solving 2x+1=7.

AM15F-04.bounds: The ratio must exceed 1 (6.4 > 4.4); all four options do. The bound that would kill 1.45 and 2 -- 'one magnitude step is a factor of 10, and there are 2 steps, so the ratio is at least 10' -- IS the tested insight, so it is not free.
issues: Thin for a partially-informed solver: anyone who knows the scale is multiplicative is down to {20, 100} without computing, and 20 vs 100 is then the only live discrimination. Not a drop -- the eliminating knowledge is the skill being measured -- but the item carries less than four options of information.

AM15F-05.bounds: All four options are range statements built from the same two constants (2, 3) crossed with the two inequality directions. No free elimination; separating them requires either the monotonicity argument or two point evaluations, both of which are the item.

AM15F-06.bounds: The above-400 interval is symmetric about the vertex t = 176/32 = 5.5, and h(0)=16 < 400 forces t1 > 0, so the duration is strictly less than 2(5.5) = 11. 11.18 is out. 3, 5, 8 survive.
issues: Weak distractor: 11.18 = sqrt(125) is the gap between the two roots of t^2-11t-1=0, one of which is NEGATIVE time. No student performs that procedure -- the natural version of that error is the positive root 11.09 ('when does it land'), which the explanation does not claim. So the fourth option is doing no work: it is both out of bound and procedurally synthetic.

Repair: replace 11.18 with 4.58 = sqrt(21), from dropping the platform term (solving -16t^2+176t = 400, i.e. t^2-11t+25=0). That is a real slip, lands inside the feasible interval, and restores a fourth live option.

AM15F-07.bounds: None. Nothing in the stem bounds the slope of g without composing. (The 2|6|18 geometric chain is the shape already measured as non-predictive; not counted.)

AM15F-08.bounds: The first difference of a quadratic is linear and non-constant, so the constant option -3 is impossible without computing anything. 4a, 4a+2, 4a-8 survive; all three have the forced leading coefficient 4, so that gives no further cut.

AM15G-01.bounds: The median is the average of the two bases, so the unknown base must exceed 22. That eliminates NOTHING -- all four options exceed 22. 44 is the strict supremum (the unknown base is 2(22) minus a positive length), but reaching 2(22)=44 and then rejecting it is the same subtraction the item asks for, so it is not free.
issues: DISAGREE WITH AUTHOR'S SELF-FLAG, harmlessly: they flagged this item for the bound 'the other base must exceed 22, and 22 is not offered'. That bound removes zero options, so it is a non-finding -- and it is the weaker of the two bounds present. The live one is 44 as a supremum, which they did not name. The item is still fine; the self-report is not.

AM15G-02.bounds: With one angle fixed at 28 degrees, the second angle of a triangle may be anything below 152. All four options (45, 56, 62, 118) are triangle-feasible; the semicircle fact is required to cut any of them.

AM15G-03.bounds: Rotating a rectangle about one of its sides gives a cylinder whose radius and height are the two side lengths in SOME order, so V = pi r^2 h is either pi(3^2)(8) = 72pi or pi(8^2)(3) = 192pi. Knowing only the volume formula -- without reading which side is the axis -- eliminates 18pi (radius 1.5, available under no reading of the stem) and 24pi (pi r h, dimensionally not a volume). 2 survivors.
issues: THIN, and the thinness is structural: after the formula, the ONLY information the stem still supplies is which of the two sides is the axis -- one bit. Two of the four options are eliminated before the stem's distinguishing clause is read.

Repair: replace 24pi (pi r h) with a value produced by a procedure that still respects the volume formula, e.g. 36pi = pi(3^2)(8)/2 (cone formula applied to a cylinder) or 144pi = pi(3^2)(16) (rotating about the 8-side but doubling the axis to the full turn). Either keeps four options inside the dimensional bound.

AM15G-04.bounds: Both formulas are given and no free relation bounds the volume from the surface area without recovering r. 48pi, 162pi, 216pi, 288pi are all plausible magnitudes for a sphere of surface area 144pi.

AM15G-05.bounds: angle APB = 180 - A/2 - B/2 and angle C = 180 - A - B. Halving strictly reduces, so APB > C = 72 with no bisector arithmetic at all -- only the one subtraction that produces 72. That kills 54 and 72. Survivors: 95 and 126.
issues: ENDPOINT DEFECT: 72 is not merely wrong, it is exactly the strict infimum of angle APB. The distractor the item most wants to punish (ignore the bisectors, report angle C) is free to eliminate by the single observation that a half-angle is smaller than the angle. 54 (the sum of the half-angles) is below the same bound.
This is the monotonicity-shaped bound the previous batch's author also missed; it is not a geometric inequality and does not look like one.

Repair: replace 54 with 103 = 180 - 62/2 - 46, the mirror of the existing 95 distractor (bisect B but use the full A). 103 lies above the 72 infimum, so survivors go to 3 {95, 103, 126}. Optionally also move 72 to 149 = 180 - 62/2 (bisect B, drop A entirely) if a third above-bound option is wanted, though 72 has real diagnostic value and the item is acceptable at 3.

AM15G-06.bounds: Cone volume increases with radius at least linearly and decreases linearly with height, so tripling r and halving h gives V_new >= 108 x 3 x 0.5 = 162, with equality only under the (wrong) linear-in-r reading. That eliminates 24 and 54 outright -- both are BELOW the original 108 -- and puts 162 exactly on the bound. Only 486 is strictly inside.
issues: Both discarded options are smaller than the original volume, which no solver who knows the radius was tripled would accept. The remaining pair is the key and the exact linear-scaling endpoint, so the item reduces to a single yes/no on 'does r enter squared' -- which it already tested, with no cover.
This is NOT the pre-cleared geometric-chain shape (24|54|162|486 being a x3 chain). The mechanism here is scaling monotonicity: two options sit on the wrong side of V_new > V_old.

Repair: replace 24 and 54 with 972 = 108 x 9 (radius squared, height change forgotten) and 1458 = 108 x 27 x 0.5 (radius factor cubed). Both are above the 162 endpoint, both from procedures already in the item's own vocabulary, and survivors return to 4.

AM15G-07.bounds: A regular hexagon of side 8 is visibly larger than a single equilateral triangle of side 8 (and than an 8-by-8 square, area 64), so 16sqrt3 = 27.7 is free to eliminate. 64sqrt3 = 110.9, 96sqrt3 = 166.3 and 192 all survive.
issues: Secondary, recorded but not spent: the hexagon strictly contains the s-by-s*sqrt3 rectangle formed by two opposite sides, area 8(8sqrt3) = 64sqrt3, so 64sqrt3 is a strict lower bound and sits exactly on it. Likewise the circumscribed circle gives area < 64pi = 201, which 192 clears only narrowly. Neither bound is free for an ACT solver (both need the apothem or the long-diagonal geometry), so the count stays 3 -- but 64sqrt3 is an endpoint and a future numeric edit should not tighten it further.

AM15G-08.bounds: Every vertex of a convex 14-gon sends the SAME number d of diagonals, and each diagonal is counted from both ends, so the total is 14d/2 = 7d -- a multiple of 7 -- without ever knowing that d = n-3. That eliminates 11 and 78 at once. Survivors: 77 and 84.
issues: DISAGREE WITH AUTHOR'S SELF-FLAG. They checked the total against C(14,2) = 91 and reported 91 is not offered. That bound eliminates nothing -- all four options are below 91 -- so it is the same non-finding shape as AM15G-01. The live bound is divisibility by 7, which they did not consider, and it removes half the option set.

Repair: replace 78 = (n-1)(n-2)/2 with 154 = 14 x 11, the canonical 'forgot to halve' error, which is 7 x 22 and therefore survives the divisibility cut. Survivors become 3 {77, 84, 154}. 154 is still eliminable by the weaker C(14,2)=91 ceiling, but that costs an actual computation. If a fourth in-bound option is wanted, also move 11 to 70 = 14 x 10 / 2 (excluding the opposite vertex as well as the two neighbours).
Do NOT use 91 itself as the replacement: it is the strict supremum (all vertex pairs, sides included), i.e. an endpoint defect of exactly the kind under audit.

AM15I-01.bounds: Compounding more often than annually strictly beats simple annual interest, so the answer must EXCEED 4000(1.06) = $4,240.00 -- which is offered, exactly on the bound -- and $4,060.00 is below it. At the top, $5,049.91 is a 26% one-year gain on a 6% certificate; the effective annual rate for quarterly 6% is about 6.14%, so nothing near $5,000 is admissible. The plausible band is roughly ($4,240, $4,300) and the key is the only option in it.
issues: ONE SURVIVOR. A solver who knows only that quarterly compounding adds a little to 6% -- and nothing about dividing the rate or multiplying the exponent -- selects $4,245.45 with no computation. That eliminating knowledge is adjacent to, not identical with, the tested mechanic, which is what makes the cut free.
$4,240.00 is additionally an exact endpoint: it is the infimum of the compounded value, attained only in the annual-compounding limit.

Repair: replace $4,060.00 with an in-band value from a named procedure -- $4,246.71 = 4000(1 + 0.06/12)^12 (read 'quarterly' as monthly) or $4,247.35 = 4000e^0.06 (continuous compounding). Either puts a second option inside the plausible band and makes the cent-level arithmetic load-bearing. Must not ship unrepaired.

AM15I-02.bounds: Three caps: flour 7/2 = 3.5 recipes (42 muffins), eggs 8/3 recipes (32), milk 4.5 recipes (54). Every elimination costs one of the three divisions the item exists to ask for, so none is free. 24, 32, 42, 54 all survive a costless reading.
issues: AUTHOR'S SELF-FLAG VERIFIED AND AGREED. 54 is exactly the milk cap, so it does sit on the bound 'output <= milk cap' -- but that cap is the LARGEST of the three and therefore never binding, so the bound it lies on removes nothing by itself. Rejecting 54 requires computing a SECOND cap, which is precisely the comparison being tested. Their reasoning is right and the option should stay.

Minor ambiguity, guarded: 8/3 recipes consumes 2 2/3 eggs. The clause 'may prepare any fraction of the recipe' is what makes 24 (the whole-recipe reading) wrong rather than defensible, and it is doing real work -- do not edit it out.

AM15I-03.bounds: A Celsius change is numerically smaller than the corresponding Fahrenheit change, so 45 (the raw Fahrenheit rise) is out on general temperature familiarity. 7.22, 13, 25 survive a strictly free reading.
issues: Soft one-survivor risk, short of a drop: the answer is 5/9 of 45, i.e. a bit more than half. The other two survivors are 7.22 and 13, both far below half of 45, so any solver who estimates 'a Celsius change is roughly half the Fahrenheit change' lands on 25 alone. I do not count that as a free cut because the 5/9-with-no-offset fact IS the tested insight -- but nothing else occupies the plausible band.

Repair: replace 13 (= 45 - 32) with 27 (= 59 - 32), the same 'subtract 32 and stop' error applied to the higher reading instead of to the difference. 27 sits inside the 20-30 band, so the estimate no longer decides the item on its own.

AM15I-04.bounds: The store profits, so the selling price exceeds the $72 cost: $54.00 is out for free. $90.00, $96.00, $112.50 survive.
issues: Recorded, not counted: because the profit is a percent of the LARGER base, the selling price must exceed 72(1.25) = $90.00, making $90.00 a strict lower bound and leaving two options. That cut is exactly the insight the item measures (base = selling price, not cost), so it is not free and the item is sound as written.

AM15I-05.bounds: 3/5 > 1/2, so the point lies strictly beyond the midpoint of A and B, which is (-4+11)/2 = 3.5 -- and 3.5 is offered, exactly on that bound. It is also below 11. Survivors: 5, 6.6, 9.
issues: ENDPOINT, reported as the prompt requires: 3.5 is not merely outside the admissible interval, it is its exact infimum. The observation that costs it is 'three fifths is more than a half', which involves none of the item's arithmetic. 5, 6.6 and 9 sit at 0.60, 0.71 and 0.87 of the way, so the remaining three still require real estimation to separate and I would not spend a repair here; if one is made, move 3.5 to 3.8 (= -4 + (3/5)(11+2), mis-taking the span as 13) so no option sits on the midpoint.

AM15I-06.bounds: Two free cuts. (i) The base is below 100, so a rise of 6 percentage points is necessarily MORE than a 6% relative increase -- 6% is out with no arithmetic. (ii) 87% would require support to rise from 40% to about 75%; the stem's rise is 6 points, so 87% is out on magnitude. Survivors: 13% and 15%.
issues: THIN, and the surviving pair is exactly {wrong base, right base} -- the item's whole discrimination with no cover around it. Half the option set is removed before any division is performed.

Repair: replace 87% with 14% = 6/43, the increase measured against the AVERAGE of the two levels (a real convention and a real student error). Survivors go to 3 {13%, 14%, 15%} and the choice of denominator becomes load-bearing at the arithmetic level, not just the magnitude level.

AM15I-07.bounds: The total exceeds the longest piece, which itself exceeds the stated 35-centimetre gap, so the total is greater than 35 and 21 is impossible with no arithmetic. 56, 105, 175 survive; nothing free separates them (rejecting 56 as 'the longest piece, not the total' requires solving for x).

AM15I-08.bounds: A 14-inch-radius wheel is about 88 inches -- 7.3 feet -- around, and a mile is 5,280 feet, so the count is in the high hundreds. It does not even need the circumference: any solver who knows a bicycle wheel turns hundreds of times per mile eliminates 20, 60 and 103 together. 720 is the only option within two orders of magnitude of the answer.
issues: ONE SURVIVOR, and by the crudest possible bound -- physical plausibility, requiring none of the tested content (circumference formula, two-step unit conversion). This is the single worst item in the batch on Priority 1. As written, the conversions the stem carefully supplies (12 inches per foot, 5,280 feet per mile) are decoration.
The three distractors also fail the magnitude sanity check that any real student applies: 20 revolutions per mile implies a wheel 264 feet around.

Repair, if kept: every distractor must land in the 300-1,500 band from a named procedure. Replace 20 with 360 (used the 28-inch DIAMETER in place of the radius, C = 2pi(28) = 175.9 inches) and 60 with 1,440 (used C = pi r instead of C = 2 pi r). 103 (divided by the wheel's AREA) is the only distractor whose procedure is worth keeping, but it too is out of band; if a third in-band procedure can be found, use it. Minimum acceptable repair is the 20 -> 360 and 60 -> 1,440 swap. Left unrepaired, drop.
